_comment: Tier 4 — the entries no API will ever cover. A human confirms each one and
signs it with a date; nothing here auto-publishes.
sensitivity   public     openly promoted by the community or tourism board
restricted real but access-controlled; coordinates blurred
sacred     not offered to outsiders; NEVER published, whatever
lastVerifiedAt drives confidence decay. Let it age and the entry fades from
the map on its own, then surfaces in the review queue asking for a human.
operatorSignals are the proxy the pipeline watches: specialist operators
publish dated departures months before the community announces anything.

events.name: Naghol (Land Diving)
events.description: Men dive from wooden towers up to 30m with only forest vines at the ankles, timed to the yam harvest. The rite the modern bungee jump was copied from.
events.consent: Villages sell scheduled visitor access through the Vanuatu Tourism Office; dates set by elders around the yam harvest.
events.notes: Saturdays through the season. Exact dates are announced locally, often only days ahead.

events.name: Gerewol
events.description: Wodaabe men dance the yaake in ochre and beads for hours in the heat, judged by women of the clan. Held where herding groups converge as the rains end.
events.consent: Attend only with Wodaabe hosts or the specialist operators who arrange with them. No fixed public venue exists.
events.notes: Nomadic and weather-dependent — the gathering point shifts year to year, so coordinates are country-level on purpose.

events.name: Goroka Show
events.description: Over a hundred highland sing-sing groups in full regalia, the largest tribal gathering in Papua New Guinea.
events.consent: Ticketed public festival with an official organising committee.

sources.name: Papua New Guinea Tourism Promotion Authority

events.notes: Held around PNG's Independence Day weekend in mid-September.

events.name: Mount Hagen Cultural Show
events.description: Western Highlands sing-sing, staged the month before Goroka and generally less crowded with visitors.

sources.name: Papua New Guinea Tourism Promotion Authority

events.notes: Third weekend of August in most years.

events.name: Timkat (Ethiopian Epiphany)
events.description: Replicas of the Ark are carried to water by torchlight and the crowd is mass-baptised at dawn; Gondar's stone bath is the focal point.
events.consent: Public religious festival, UNESCO-inscribed and openly attended.
events.notes: Falls on 20 January in Ethiopian leap years.

events.name: Hornbill Festival
events.description: Seventeen Naga tribes gather at Kisama for a week of morungs, log drums and dance — a state-organised meeting of groups that were once hostile.
events.consent: Organised by the Nagaland state tourism department.
events.notes: Protected Area Permit rules for foreign visitors change periodically — re-check before each season.

events.name: Inti Raymi
events.description: Reconstructed Inca sun festival at Sacsayhuamán on the southern winter solstice, staged for a crowd in the tens of thousands.
events.consent: Municipal public event with ticketed seating.
events.notes: Fixed civic date, unlike the astronomical solstice a few days earlier.

events.name: Dia de Muertos
events.description: Families keep vigil at gravesides through the night with marigolds, candles and the food the dead preferred.
events.consent: Public observance; cemetery vigils are family occasions where visitors are expected to be unobtrusive.
events.notes: Village cemeteries around Oaxaca differ sharply from the city's tourist-heavy comparsas.

events.name: Hopi village ceremonies
events.description: Recorded so the pipeline knows to stay silent. Most Hopi ceremonies have been closed to non-Hopi for decades, and the villages ask that dates and locations not be circulated.
events.consent: None, and none sought. The villages have publicly asked outsiders to stay away from these observances.
events.notes: Deliberate negative entry: reviewStatus is 'published' and it still must never reach the map. If this ever appears in output, the sensitivity gate is broken.
